What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make

Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation-time interventions on Qwen3-4B-Base, measuring how much of its RL-trained counterpart’s gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192-token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model’s token only where the two models’ greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH-500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with “Alright” recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as “Wait” do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model’s diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model’s diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/CyrusZhang04/WhatRLBrings.


 

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard way to turn a pretrained language model into a strong mathematical reasoner (Lambert et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Shao and others, 2024). Its performance gains are substantial, yet what RL adds to the base model remains unclear. Whether it teaches new reasoning abilities or mainly brings out ones the base model already has is still debated (Yue et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025). Understanding this distinction requires identifying which changes in the model’s behavior account for the improvement.

We start from differences visible in the generated responses. Our main comparison uses Qwen3-4B-Base and its GRPO-trained counterpart. On AIME, the RL model opens consistently with “Alright, I have this problem…” and produces only 3.2 distinct openings among 16 responses, compared with 15.6 for the base model. It also reflects more and writes longer responses, using “Wait” about 5.7 times per response against 0.3 for the base model. These observations accompany broader findings that RL can sharply reduce entropy (Cui et al., 2025), lose its advantage over the base model at large kk (Yue et al., 2025), and concentrate its changes at a small set of high-entropy tokens (Wang et al., 2025b; Meng et al., 2026).

These observations describe what changes, not which change produces the gain. Sharpening the base distribution, changing a few token choices, and altering the use of reflective behaviors have each been linked to improved reasoning (Karan and Du, 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Venhoff et al., 2025). However, evidence from different models, benchmarks and generation budgets does not establish how much each accounts for in the same setting. We therefore turn observed differences into interventions on the base model and ask five questions:

  1. 1.

    Can power sampling reproduce the RL gain by sharpening the base distribution (Test 0)?

  2. 2.

    Can most of the gain be recovered by changing only a small fraction of token choices (Test 1)?

  3. 3.

    How much of this gain comes from the opening token, and how much from later choices (Test 2)?

  4. 4.

    Can fixed rules over reflective tokens reproduce the benefit of the later choices (Test 3)?

  5. 5.

    Can the RL accuracy gain be retained without the same loss of diversity?

We study these questions on the 120 problems of AIME 2022–2025 using Qwen3-4B-Base and its GRPO-trained counterpart, where RL raises pass@1 from 10.00% to 19.32%. Under the tested configuration and the 8,192-token output limit, power sampling does not consistently outperform greedy decoding. A decoder we call rl-replace recovers 90.5% of the RL gain by taking the RL model’s greedy token where the two models’ greedy choices differ, about 4% of generated positions, and sampling from the base model elsewhere. The gap between power sampling and sparse replacement also holds across three model pairs on MATH-500.

Using rl-replace as a reference, we find that forcing the opening token “Alright” alone recovers 35% of the RL gain, while later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1. Neither base-greedy replacement nor the tested reflective-token rules reproduce the full benefit. Sparse replacement also preserves greater output diversity than the RL model and achieves higher pass@256 than both the RL model and a response-level mixture matched in pass@1. A similar accuracy–coverage pattern holds for Qwen3-8B. These coverage comparisons use equal attempt counts; rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step.

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We show that sparse token replacement can retain most of the RL accuracy gain alongside greater output diversity, while improving large-kk coverage over the RL model and a response-level mixture matched in pass@1.

  2. 2.

    We quantify the contribution of the opening and the additional benefit of later RL choices, and show that base-greedy replacement and the tested reflective-token rules do not reproduce the full benefit.

  3. 3.

    We provide a common intervention protocol for comparing explanations of the RL gain, and establish a substantial gap between power sampling and sparse replacement across three model pairs on MATH-500.

2 Related Work

What does RL add to a base model?

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (Lambert et al., 2024), typically with GRPO (Shao and others, 2024) or DAPO (Yu and others, 2025), is now standard for improving mathematical reasoning (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Kimi Team et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025), but whether it teaches new abilities remains debated (Liu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025). Base models catch up with their RL-trained counterparts in pass@kk at large kk (Yue et al., 2025), suggesting RL mainly makes the base model produce solutions it could already find (Zhao et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c; Matsutani et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), at the cost of diversity (Cui et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b). Reasoning behaviors such as backtracking and verification already exist in base models (Gandhi et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b), and Venhoff et al. (2025) find thinking models mainly learn when to use them. Reflective tokens such as “Wait” carry answer information (Qian et al., 2025) and can extend thinking (Muennighoff et al., 2025), but suppressing them shortens outputs without lowering accuracy (Wang et al., 2025a), and more reflection does not always help (Kang et al., 2025; Ghosal et al., 2025; Gema et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025d; Chen et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025). We compare these explanations side by side, intervening on the base model of one RL model on hard competition problems.

Reasoning from the base model without training.

A related line seeks RL-level reasoning from the base model directly (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Wang and Zhou, 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025). Karan and Du (2025) sample from the sharpened distribution pbaseαp_{\text{base}}^{\alpha} with MCMC and report results close to GRPO on MATH-500; later work changes where the sampler resamples (Zhou et al., 2026) and shows that sharpening can lower majority-vote accuracy (Yang et al., 2026) and that Best-of-NN recovers most of its gains (Talwar et al., 2026). Wang et al. (2026) show a short opening cue from training data, such as “Alright” for Qwen3, recovers much of the RL gain. We test both as explanations of the RL gain on hard problems at the RL model’s generation budget (Tests 0 and 2).

Token-level analysis of RL.

The effect of RL is sparse (Mukherjee et al., 2025) and concentrated on a few high-entropy decision tokens (Wang et al., 2025b), much as alignment changes only a few tokens (Lin et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023; Qi et al., 2024), and substituting the RL model’s tokens at such positions recovers most of its accuracy (Meng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Akgül et al., 2026). Our Test 1 uses such substitution, a decoding-time combination of two models (Liu et al., 2024; Mitchell et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Fei et al., 2024; Leviathan et al., 2022), as a reference rather than a finding. We ask how its gain divides between opening and later tokens, whether later tokens can be produced by fixed rules, and whether it keeps the base model’s diversity.

3 Analysis: Testing Explanations of the RL Gain

We compare interventions by the fraction of the RL pass@1 gain they recover, defined below. Figure 1 summarizes the diagnostic tests, and Figure 3 reports their results on AIME. Because intervention effects may overlap, recovery rates should not be interpreted as independent causal contributions that sum to the total gain. Section 3.6 then examines whether the recovered accuracy gain can coexist with greater output diversity and coverage at larger sampling budgets.

3.1 Setup

Models.

Our analysis centers on Qwen3-4B-Base (Yang and others, 2025) and an RL model trained from it directly, without supervised fine-tuning, using GRPO (Shao and others, 2024) on DAPO-Math-17k (Yu and others, 2025) in verl (Sheng et al., 2024). To avoid train–test contamination, we removed all problems duplicating AIME 2022 or 2023 from the DAPO training set prior to RL training. We keep the checkpoint with the highest accuracy on a validation split of DAPO-Math-17k (step 460), so no evaluation benchmark is used for checkpoint selection. RL raises MATH-500 pass@1 from 71.1% to 84.4% (Table 1). Tests 0 and 1 are repeated on MATH-500 with Qwen3-8B-Base and Llama-3.2-3B (Grattafiori and others, 2024), whose RL models are trained with the same recipe. Training hyperparameters are listed in Appendix A.

Benchmarks and decoding.

Our main benchmark is the 120 problems of AIME 2022–2025, reported for AIME24+25, AIME22+23 and all 120 problems; MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2023) serves as an easier benchmark. Every model and intervention receives the same prompt, which asks for the final answer in \boxed{} (Appendix B). We sample at temperature 0.6 with top-pp 0.95 and at most 8,192 tokens, and grade the last boxed answer with Math-Verify (Kydlíček and Hugging Face, 2025).

Sample budgets and metrics.

On AIME we draw 16 samples per problem for every model and intervention, and on MATH-500 we draw 64. pass@1 is the mean accuracy over all samples, and pass@kk is the fraction of problems solved by at least one of kk samples, computed with the unbiased estimator of Chen and others (2021) when kk is smaller than the number of samples. The power-sampling comparison runs standard sampling and MCMC with 8 seeds and greedy decoding once, and the large-kk comparison of §3.6 draws 512 samples per problem from the base and RL models and 256 from rl-replace. To compare interventions we use the recovery rate,

R⁡(method)=pass@1​(method)−pass@1​(base)pass@1​(RL)−pass@1​(base),R(\text{method})=\frac{\text{pass@1}(\text{method})-\text{pass@1}(\text{base})}{\text{pass@1}(\text{RL})-\text{pass@1}(\text{base})}, (1)

with 95% confidence intervals from a problem-level bootstrap (10,000 resamples within each problem group). Differences between two conditions are resampled on the same problems (Appendix C).

rl-replace.

Test 1 relies on a decoder that we call rl-replace: whenever the two models prefer different next tokens, it takes the RL model’s choice, and otherwise it keeps sampling from the base model. Formally, let pBp_{B} and pRp_{R} denote the base and RL models. At each step tt with prefix y<ty_{<t}, we compute the two greedy tokens bt=argmaxpB(⋅∣y<t)b_{t}=\arg\max p_{B}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}) and rt=argmaxpR(⋅∣y<t)r_{t}=\arg\max p_{R}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}). If bt≠rtb_{t}\neq r_{t} we emit rtr_{t}; otherwise we sample yt∼pB(⋅∣y<t)y_{t}\sim p_{B}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}) at temperature 0.6. The RL model therefore only intervenes at the positions where the two models’ preferred next tokens differ, which we call disagreement positions, and the base model writes everything else (Figure 4). Because both models run at every step, rl-replace costs 7.3–7.9 GPU-hours per AIME year, and we use it as a diagnostic of where the gain lies rather than as a practical decoding method. Appendix A gives the full procedure and the settings of every experiment.

3.2 Test 0: can power sampling recover the RL gain?

We first ask how much of the RL gain can be recovered by sharpening the base distribution alone. We use the power-sampling MCMC of Karan and Du (2025), which targets pbaseαp_{\text{base}}^{\alpha} with α=4\alpha=4, 16 blocks and 10 MCMC steps per block, following the original paper. All methods have the same 8,192-token output limit.

Table 1 shows two regimes. On MATH-500, MCMC improves pass@1 over standard sampling by 2.35–3.50 percentage points across all three base models, consistent with Karan and Du (2025). For Qwen3-4B-Base, however, this improvement does not increase observed problem coverage with eight samples per problem. MCMC solves 400 of the 500 problems in at least one of its 8 seeds, compared with 408 for standard sampling (pass@8 of 80.0% and 81.6%). Only two problems are solved by MCMC alone, against ten by standard sampling alone. The higher pass@1 therefore mainly reflects more reliable success on problems also solved by standard sampling. Even on MATH-500, rl-replace and RL remain approximately 8–12 points above MCMC across all three models.

On AIME, MCMC provides no consistent gain over standard sampling and does not meaningfully outperform greedy decoding. For Qwen3-4B-Base, MCMC improves over standard sampling on AIME25 (13.75% versus 9.58%), but reaches essentially the same accuracy as greedy decoding (13.33%). On AIME24, it stays near standard sampling and below greedy decoding. For Qwen3-8B-Base, MCMC falls below both standard sampling and greedy decoding on both benchmarks: it obtains 16.67% on AIME24 and 20.42% on AIME25, compared with greedy accuracies of 20.00% and 23.33%. Across the four model–benchmark pairs, rl-replace and RL exceed MCMC by approximately 5–14 points. Supplementary experiments on AIME 2022–2024 also show MCMC matching standard sampling at 10.00% (Appendix D).

The long generations expose additional difficulties for the sampler. Relative to standard sampling, the fraction of AIME responses with no final answer rises from 12.2% to 22.4%, and the fraction ending in repetition rises from 6.7% to 13.1%. Restricting MCMC to positions that a learned gate marks as likely high-KL positions (Appendix E) does not help either: on the 120 AIME problems, this variant obtains 9.84 / 24.17 pass@1 / pass@16, compared with 10.00 / 30.00 for standard base sampling.

These results identify a limit of power sampling under the tested configuration and output-length limit. Sharpening the base distribution improves pass@1 on MATH-500, but does not recover the RL gain on AIME for either Qwen model size. Applying the sampler selectively at predicted high-KL positions also brings no gain. This leaves a more specific question: how much of the gain can be recovered by borrowing the RL model’s choices at only a small fraction of positions?

3.3 Test 1: is the gain localized at a few positions?

We test this with rl-replace, which borrows the RL model’s choice only where the two models’ greedy tokens differ. On all 120 problems, it raises pass@1 from 10.00% to 18.44%, against 19.32% for the RL model, recovering 90.5% of the gain (Table 2). The recovery is similar on AIME24+25 (92.1%) and AIME22+23 (87.7%); the difference of 4.4 points has a 95% interval of [−32,+41][-32,+41] and is not significant.

The intervention is sparse. The RL model’s token is used at about 4.0% of all generated tokens (4.5% when averaged per response), and the remaining 96% are written by the base model. On MATH-500, rl-replace recovers the full RL gain (106.6%), and it recovers most of the gain for the two other model pairs as well (§4.1). Meng et al. (2026) report a similar finding with a divergence-based cross-sampling procedure.

Sparse describes how many tokens are borrowed, not how far their effect reaches. Each borrowed token becomes part of the prefix the base model continues from, so an early choice can change everything the base model writes after it. This shows in the length of the responses: rl-replace responses average 6,217 tokens, close to the RL model’s 6,504 and nearly twice the base model’s 3,248 (Appendix F.1). A few local decisions are thus enough to redirect the whole response, while every other token is still sampled from the base model. We use rl-replace as the reference for the next two tests. The first replacement is especially conspicuous: every response begins with the same word. We next isolate how much this opening contributes before examining the later choices.

3.4 Test 2: how much does the opening contribute?

Every one of the 1,920 rl-replace responses on the 120 problems starts with “Alright”, the first word of the RL model’s usual opening, “Alright, I have this problem…”. The base model opens in varied ways, often by computing immediately or by continuing the chat template. This consistent first-token replacement suggests a simple intervention: force the base model to begin with “Alright” (or “Alright, I”) and let it generate the rest without any help from the RL model.

Comparing this opening-only intervention with the base model measures what the cue itself contributes. Comparing it with rl-replace, which starts with the same word, measures the additional benefit of the later replacements. A third condition uses the same opening and disagreement rule as rl-replace but emits the base model’s own greedy token at disagreements, allowing us to compare the benefit of committing to a token with that of using the RL model’s choice.

Table 4 gives three findings. First, a single opening token recovers a substantial part of the RL gain. Forcing “Alright” raises pass@1 from 10.00% to 13.23%, recovering 35% of the gain, and raises pass@16 from 30.00% to 35.00%. Extending the prefix to “Alright, I” adds no further improvement. In our setting, the opening provides a simple way to recover part of the gain, while leaving a substantial gap to the RL model.

Second, the later replacements contribute even more. Beyond the same opening, rl-replace adds 5.2 percentage points to pass@1 (95% CI [3.1,7.6][3.1,7.6]), equivalent to 56% of the RL gain. The opening and later replacements together recover 90.5%, compared with 35% from the opening alone.

Third, choosing the base model’s own greedy token recovers only a small part of this additional benefit. At a disagreement position, rl-replace both stops sampling and uses the RL model’s token. Applying the same rule but emitting the base model’s greedy token gives 14.74%, 1.5 points above the opening alone and 3.7 below rl-replace. The larger gain therefore comes from using the RL model’s choices, beyond the benefit of committing to a token under the same disagreement rule.

These comparisons measure the later replacements after an “Alright” opening; their benefit may include interactions with the opening, which we do not separate. Having established that later choices add more than the opening alone, we next examine what these choices look like and whether fixed rules can reproduce their benefit.

3.5 Test 3: can fixed reflective-token rules recover the gain?

What the later replacements look like.

We examine the 19 problems on which the base model fails all 16 samples while rl-replace solves at least one. The 38 successful rl-replace responses contain 9,099 replacements that change the text (the rest only change tokenization). Table 4 groups them by type, and Appendix F gives the per-problem details. Most (74.7%) are ordinary content-word changes, such as paraphrases and wording; opening and pause words such as “Wait”, together with the prefix “Re”, make up only 2.6%. We focus the rule-based tests on these visible tokens because they are easy to imitate and often associated with reflective behavior after RL (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Gandhi et al., 2025).

Replacements occur throughout the response but are more frequent near the beginning: the first 20% contains 26.1% of all replacements, while the 60–70% segment contains the smallest share (7.8%). The category distribution is almost identical on the problems the RL model solves on its own and on those it does not (all categories within 0.5 points).

A few recurring patterns stand out. The RL model writes “Wait” where the base model’s greedy token is “So”, “But” or a section header (So→\toWait 20 times, But→\toWait 8, ###→\toWait 30), as after a total in one successful response (RL token in brackets):

Total = 404 + 405 = 809.
[Wait], but we need to ensure that we are not double-counting.

It also restructures the solution with a new header (Let→\to### and But→\to###, 24 times), typically right after such a pause, and turns a conclusion into a check (So→\toBut, 20 times). Number replacements show no fixed preference and depend on context, for example changing a value that violates a constraint stated earlier in the problem. Appendix I.2 shows a response in which a ###→\toWait replacement is followed by an overlap check and the correct answer. These examples motivate a narrower test: can simple rules that insert the same reflective tokens recover some of the gain?

Inserting the same tokens by rule.

We build rules from the tokens the RL model uses and apply them to the base model without consulting the RL model during generation (Table 5). Hard rules force a token at a trigger position. The triggers were derived from statistics of where the two models disagree, using a predictor of high-KL positions that relies only on the base model’s own confidence (Appendix E). The “Wait” rule fires when the base model emits a section header right after a formula block, and the “Re” rule uses an analogous trigger for the reflective prefix. Soft rules add a constant to the logit of “Re” instead of forcing it.

Every hard rule falls well below the base model, by 5.5–7.7 points on pass@1 and 9–22 points on pass@16, and combining the rules is worst. A fixed trigger applies the same edit at the same kind of position across samples, whether or not a check is needed. For example, a section header after a formula block can mark an ordinary transition; forcing a pause there can interrupt reasoning that was on track. Soft rules bring no improvement either. Their pass@1 is 1.5 points below the base model, a difference within the variation we observe between independent base-model runs (§4.2), and the two bias strengths give nearly identical results.

Type Condition pass@1 pass@16
– Base 10.00 30.00
Hard Force “Wait” 4.48 20.83
Force “Re” 4.32 10.83
Force “Wait” and “Re” 2.29 08.33
Soft “Re” logit +2+2 8.54 24.17
“Re” logit +4+4 8.49 24.17

Other rule-like interventions lead to the same conclusion (Appendix G). Forcing “Wait” whenever it appears among the base model’s top-5 candidates lowers accuracy to 6.25%, and all 282 responses that receive six or more insertions are wrong, even though the RL model itself uses about 5.7 “Wait”s per response. Forcing “Wait” after an “Alright” opening collapses accuracy to 0.26%. Raising the probability of first-person pronouns, decoding the first 100 tokens greedily or at low temperature, and stopping early based on entropy all leave accuracy at the base level. On a small set of the hardest problems, replacing the RL token at the disagreement positions with a random base candidate yields 0 correct responses out of 480, compared with 3 out of 480 when the RL token is used; we treat this last comparison as qualitative given its size.

Together, these results show that merely increasing the frequency of the RL model’s reflective tokens via fixed rules does not reproduce the accuracy benefit of sparse replacement, even though the rules raise the frequency of ’Wait’ well above the base model’s own usage (0.3 per response). The gap suggests that what rl-replace transfers is not reflective tokens as such, but the right reflective tokens at the right positions—along with many non-reflective content-word changes. One possibility is that RL sharpens the model’s sense of when its reasoning has gone wrong, rather than teaching it to reflect unconditionally. To test the more specific view that RL learns when to deploy existing behaviors (Venhoff et al., 2025), one could retain only the reflective replacements at positions chosen by the RL model and compare them with a rule that fires equally often. Our negative result is limited to the fixed rules tested here; we do not evaluate learned or entropy-based selection schemes such as that of Akgül et al. (2026).

3.6 Is the gain tied to the loss of diversity?

The preceding tests show that sparse replacement recovers most of the RL accuracy gain. We now ask whether this recovery also requires the RL model’s loss of output diversity. Table 6 reports the large-kk results for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, while Figure 5 shows the Qwen3-4B curves for all 120 AIME problems and for the two problem groups.

Accuracy and output diversity.

For Qwen3-4B, rl-replace stays close to the RL model at pass@1 in the large-kk run (18.98% versus 19.77%). The diversity statistics from the main run, measured over 16 responses per problem, show a different pattern. The base model produces an average of 15.6 distinct openings, defined as the first 300 characters, compared with 3.2 for the RL model and 9.7 for rl-replace. The corresponding numbers of distinct final answers are 9.42, 7.98, and 8.82. Sparse replacement therefore retains greater output diversity than the RL model while recovering most of its accuracy gain.

Coverage at larger sampling budgets.

Prior work finds that the RL model’s advantage at pass@1 can disappear as kk grows (Yue et al., 2025). Our Qwen3-4B pair follows this pattern: the RL model leads the base model by 8.4–9.5 percentage points from k=1k=1 to k=64k=64, but the lead shrinks to 4.6 points at k=128k=128 and disappears at k=256k=256 (61.40% versus 61.64%).

In contrast, rl-replace reaches 67.50% at k=256k=256 (Figure 5a). Its advantage over the RL model grows from 0.13 points at k=4k=4 to 2.28 at k=16k=16 and 6.10 at k=256k=256; the last difference has a 95% confidence interval of [0.82,11.02][0.82,11.02]. Its observed advantage over the base model is 5.86 points, although the corresponding interval, [−0.33,10.71][-0.33,10.71], includes zero. Thus, the large-kk results support a coverage advantage over the RL model, while the comparison with the base model remains less certain.

Comparison with a response-level mixture.

Could mixing whole responses obtain the same combination of accuracy and coverage? We test a mixture that independently selects the RL model with probability 0.92 and the base model otherwise for each attempt. The weight is chosen to approximately match rl-replace at pass@1: 19.00% versus 18.98%. The generation procedure is described in Appendix H.

The mixture remains close to the RL model, reaching 38.78% at k=16k=16 and 61.45% at k=256k=256. At the latter budget, rl-replace leads by 6.05 percentage points (95% CI [0.93,10.98][0.93,10.98]). At approximately matched pass@1, combining the models within each response therefore achieves higher pass@256 than the response-level mixture tested here. These comparisons use equal numbers of attempts: rl-replace runs both models at every decoding step, whereas the mixture uses only one model per response.

Problem groups and model size.

The Qwen3-4B coverage advantage over the RL model is observed in both problem groups, although it emerges at different budgets. On AIME24+25, rl-replace leads by 5.2–7.3 points from k=16k=16 onward and reaches 70.00% at k=256k=256, compared with 62.98% for the RL model and 63.67% for the base model (Figure 5b). On AIME22+23, the RL model is slightly ahead through k=64k=64, but rl-replace overtakes it from k=128k=128 onward, reaching 65.00% versus 59.81% at k=256k=256 (Figure 5c).

Qwen3-8B shows a similar accuracy–coverage pattern (Table 6). rl-replace remains close to the RL model at pass@1 (27.16% versus 28.32%) and achieves higher observed pass@256: 72.50%, compared with 66.82% for the RL model and 68.33% for the base model.

Temperature sensitivity.

Changing the Qwen3-4B RL model’s temperature does not close the observed coverage gap. Among temperatures 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8 at fixed top-p=0.95p=0.95, the original setting of 0.6 gives the highest RL pass@256. The full results are reported in Appendix H.1.

Implications for interpreting the RL gain.

Yue et al. (2025) interpret their coverage and reasoning-path analyses as evidence that current RLVR primarily improves sampling efficiency over reasoning paths already available to the base model. Our results highlight a distinction between the coverage of the RL model under its own decoding distribution and the usefulness of its token choices within a different generation policy. By selectively incorporating these choices, rl-replace recovers most of the RL accuracy gain while retaining greater output diversity and achieving higher pass@256 than the RL model and the response-level mixture tested here. This suggests that beneficial changes in token preferences can be retained without reproducing the full reduction in output diversity observed in the RL model.

These findings do not establish that RL creates reasoning paths unavailable to the base model: rl-replace is a hybrid generation policy, and finite-budget pass@kk does not identify the full set of paths a model can generate. Nor do they establish diversity loss as the cause of the coverage difference. Rather, they show that the RL model’s own large-kk coverage does not fully characterize the value of the decisions it contributes to reasoning.

4 Robustness

Our detailed intervention analysis centers on Qwen3-4B and a main run with 16 samples per problem on 120 AIME problems. We assess robustness across additional model pairs (Section 4.1), individual competition years and independent runs (Section 4.2). Larger sample budgets for both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B are reported in Section 3.6.

4.1 Other model pairs

We repeat Tests 0 and 1 on MATH-500 with the two additional base/RL pairs, Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-3B, whose RL models are trained with the same recipe as the 4B model (§3.1); their pass@1 values are in Table 1. The two tests give the same answer for all three pairs. Measured against standard base sampling, sharpening recovers 17.7%, 19.2% and 26.7% of the RL gain for Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-3B, while borrowing the RL model’s choice at the disagreement positions recovers 106.6%, 88.6% and 86.5%. The gap between Tests 0 and 1 is therefore not specific to Qwen3-4B, nor to a particular model family.

We also evaluate Qwen3-8B on AIME24 and AIME25 in the power-sampling comparison (Table 1), and on all 120 AIME problems in the large-kk comparison (Table 6). In the latter, rl-replace stays close to the RL model at pass@1 (27.16% versus 28.32%) while achieving higher observed pass@256 than either the base or RL model. These results extend the accuracy–coverage pattern to Qwen3-8B. The opening and reflective-token ablations in Sections 3.4–3.5 remain limited to Qwen3-4B, while Llama-3.2-3B is evaluated only on MATH-500.

4.2 Individual years and independent runs

The groups in Table 2 pool two competition years each. Table 7 breaks them down. rl-replace recovers between 85% and 100% of the RL pass@1 gain on every year, and its pass@16 is never below that of the RL model. The fraction of replaced tokens is stable across years (4.3–4.7%), so the sparsity of the intervention does not depend on the problem set. Majority voting over 16 samples (maj@16) gives a noisier picture, as expected with 30 problems per year, but rl-replace improves over the base model on every year.

Independent runs.

An earlier, independent run of the full protocol on AIME 2024 and 2025 gives the same picture: rl-replace reaches 22.08% and 20.00% pass@1 against 23.13% and 21.67% for the RL model, recovering 90.1% and 86.6% of the gain. The larger run of §3.6 (Table 6) also reproduces the main result: from its k=1k=1 values, rl-replace recovers 91.7% of the RL gain on all 120 problems (88.0% on AIME24+25 and 97.8% on AIME22+23), against 90.5% in the main run.

Run-to-run variation.

Repeated evaluations of the same model are not identical. Across our Qwen3-4B runs, the base model’s pass@1 on the 120 AIME problems ranges from approximately 8.2% to 10.26%, and the RL model’s pass@1 on AIME 2025 ranges from 20.4% to 23.3% over six evaluations. We therefore interpret small differences between independent runs cautiously. The opening-only intervention improves pass@1 by 3.2 points and pass@16 by 5.0 points, while rl-replace improves pass@1 by 8.4 points. The hard rules lower pass@1 by 5.5–7.7 points. The roughly 1.5-point decreases from the soft rules are comparable to the variation between independent runs, so we report these conditions only as bringing no observed improvement.

5 Conclusion

We asked what RL adds to a base model on hard math problems by testing common explanations of the gain with interventions on the base model. Borrowing the RL model’s token only at the positions where the two models’ greedy tokens differ recovers most of the gain, whereas sharpening the base distribution, forcing the RL model’s opening and inserting reflective tokens by fixed rules each recover at most a minority of it. Most of the gain comes after the opening: on top of the same opening, the RL model’s later choices add 5.2 points, more than half of the RL gain, and using the base model’s own greedy token at the same positions gives less than a third of this increment. These few decisions redirect the whole response, yet borrowing only them keeps much of the base model’s diversity, and with the same number of attempts rl-replace solves more problems at large kk than either model or a response-level mixture matched in pass@1. The base model’s own confidence already ranks the positions where RL changes the next-token distribution most (Appendix E); what remains hard is choosing the right token there.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 The rl-replace decoder

rl-replace generates one response at a time with the base model and the RL model reading the same prefix. Starting from the prompt of Appendix B, each step proceeds as follows.

  1. 1.

    Both models score the current prefix y<ty_{<t}, giving pB(⋅∣y<t)p_{B}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}) and pR(⋅∣y<t)p_{R}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}).

  2. 2.

    The two greedy tokens bt=argmaxpB(⋅∣y<t)b_{t}=\arg\max p_{B}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}) and rt=argmaxpR(⋅∣y<t)r_{t}=\arg\max p_{R}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}) are compared.

  3. 3.

    If bt≠rtb_{t}\neq r_{t}, the step is a disagreement position and rtr_{t} is emitted. Otherwise yty_{t} is sampled from pBp_{B} at temperature 0.6 with top-pp 0.95.

  4. 4.

    The emitted token is appended to the prefix of both models, and generation stops at the end-of-sequence token or after 8,192 tokens.

Because each RL model is trained from its own base model, the two share a tokenizer and the comparison is made on token ids. Two different ids can decode to the same text: in the 38 responses analysed in Appendix F, 9,472 tokens were emitted by the RL model, of which 9,099 (96.1%) change the text and 373 differ only in tokenization. The replace rate of a response is the number of tokens emitted by the RL model divided by the response length; the per-token rate pools all tokens of a run and gives more weight to long responses, which is why it is slightly lower (4.0%) than the per-response average (4.5%).

The rule involves no threshold. The RL model is consulted only through its greedy token, so rl-replace never samples from the RL model, and at the positions where the two greedy tokens agree the output is distributed exactly as standard base sampling.

A.2 Settings of each experiment

Table 8 summarizes the experimental settings. All evaluations use the prompt of Appendix B and a limit of 8,192 generated tokens. Unless otherwise specified, standard sampling uses temperature 0.6 and top-pp 0.95. In rl-replace, these settings apply to base-model sampling at agreement positions; disagreement positions use the RL model’s greedy token. Greedy controls, power sampling, and temperature ablations follow the settings specified in their respective sections.

A.3 RL training

Table 9 lists the training configuration shared by the three RL models. Hyperparameters not listed are the defaults of verl’s GRPO recipe.

Training dynamics.

The Qwen3-4B run follows the usual pattern of RL applied directly to a base model. Training accuracy rises from 0.071 at the first step to 0.413 at step 50 and reaches a plateau of 0.50–0.54 after about 150 steps (0.503 at step 460, the checkpoint we use). Over the same period the median rollout length grows from 521 to 3,917 tokens, and the fraction of rollouts without a valid final answer falls from 0.408 to 0.027. Training runs on 8 GPUs with FSDP, and every step draws 128 prompts with 8 rollouts each, without resampling.

A.4 Compute

All generation uses vLLM [Kwon et al., 2023] on NVIDIA H800 GPUs. rl-replace runs a forward pass of both models for every generated token, with the two models served by separate vLLM engines on the same GPU. One AIME year with 16 samples per problem takes 7.3–7.9 GPU-hours, MATH-500 about 55 GPU-hours, and the large-kk run with 256 samples per problem on all four years about 1,012 GPU-hours.

Appendix B Prompt Templates

Evaluation.

Every model and intervention in this paper is evaluated with the same two messages. For Qwen3 models, applying the chat template with thinking disabled gives the following input, where {question} is the problem statement:

<|im_start|>system
You are a helpful assistant.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
{question}
Please reason step by step, and put your final answer
within \boxed{}.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
<think>

</think>

Line breaks inside the instruction texts, here and below, are for display only. Llama-3.2-3B receives the same system and user messages through its own chat template. Interventions that prefill the response (Test 2) append the forced text directly after this input.

RL training.

RL rollouts use the prompt format distributed with DAPO-Math-17k [Yu and others, 2025], with a single user turn:

Solve the following math problem step by step. The last
line of your response should be of the form Answer: $Answer
(without quotes) where $Answer is the answer to the problem.

{question}

Remember to put your answer on its own line after "Answer:".

Appendix C Metrics and Confidence Intervals

pass@kk.

For a problem with nn samples of which cc are correct, we use the unbiased estimator of Chen and others [2021],

pass@​k=1−(n−ck)/(nk),\text{pass@}k=1-\binom{n-c}{k}\Big/\binom{n}{k}, (2)

and average it over problems. pass@1 is then the mean accuracy over all samples, and when k=nk=n the estimator reduces to the fraction of problems solved at least once. The value for all 120 AIME problems is the mean of the two groups of 60, which equals the mean over problems.

Recovery rate.

The recovery rate of §3.1 is a ratio of two pass@1 differences measured on the same problems. Its interval is obtained with a problem-level bootstrap: we draw 10,000 resamples of the problems with replacement, within each group of 60 AIME problems (or within MATH-500), recompute both differences on every resample, and take the 95% interval of the resulting ratios. Because the denominator, the RL gain, also varies across resamples, the intervals are wide and can extend above 100% even when the point estimate is below it.

Differences between conditions.

When two conditions are compared, both are evaluated on the same resampled problems, so the interval reflects only the variation of their difference across problems. Table 10 collects the intervals used in the paper.

Per-problem comparison.

The pass@1 differences in Table 2 are spread over many problems. On AIME24+25, rl-replace has a higher per-problem accuracy than the base model on 26 problems and a lower one on 4; against the RL model it is higher on 11 and lower on 13. On AIME22+23 the corresponding counts are 21 and 0 against the base model and 7 and 9 against the RL model. The numbers of problems solved at least once in 16 samples are 22, 29 and 25 on AIME24+25 and 14, 23 and 23 on AIME22+23 for the base model, rl-replace and the RL model, as reflected in the pass@16 columns of Table 2.

Majority voting.

maj@16 takes the most frequent final answer among the 16 samples of a problem, grouping answers that Math-Verify judges equivalent, and scores it against the reference answer.

Appendix D Power Sampling Details

We follow the power-sampling MCMC of Karan and Du [2025]: the target distribution is the sequence-level power distribution pbaseαp_{\text{base}}^{\alpha} with α=4\alpha=4, which differs from token-level sampling at temperature 1/α1/\alpha. Each response is generated in 16 blocks, and each block is refined with 10 MCMC steps. Standard sampling (at temperature 0.6) and MCMC use 8 seeds (0–7), and greedy decoding is run once. All runs share the 8,192-token generation limit of the main experiments.

On AIME 2022–2024, MCMC matches standard sampling and stays below greedy decoding. On AIME 2025 it matches greedy decoding. On AIME, MCMC also degrades the outputs: the fraction of responses without a final answer rises from 12.2% to 22.4%, and the fraction that ends in repetition rises from 6.7% to 13.1%.

Gate-MCMC.

The gated variant in §3.2 applies MCMC only at positions where the gradient-boosted gate of Appendix E scores at least 0.8567, which uses only the six base-model features listed there. On the 120 AIME problems with 16 samples per problem it obtains 9.84 / 24.17 pass@1 / pass@16, against 10.00 / 30.00 for standard base sampling.

Appendix E Locating High-KL Positions from the Base Model

Section 3.3 shows that the RL gain is concentrated at the few disagreement positions, where the two models’ greedy tokens differ. Here we ask whether positions where the two models diverge can be located using only the base model, without running the RL model. This predictor is used in two places in the main text: the gate in gate-MCMC (§3.2) and the trigger statistics behind the hard rules (§3.5).

Data and features.

The base model generates 16 responses to each of the 30 AIME 2024 and 30 AIME 2025 problems at temperature 0.6, and the RL model scores every prefix of these responses. The two trained predictors in Table 12, logistic regression and the gate, are fit on responses to DAPO-Math-17k problems, the data used for RL training, and all AUROC values are computed on the AIME responses. For each token we record six features computed from the base model alone: the entropy of its next-token distribution, the probability of its top candidate, the margin between its top two candidates, the log-probability of the token it actually sampled (chosen log-prob), the rank of that token, and the relative position in the response.

Labels.

We evaluate two labels for the positions where the two models differ. The KL label marks the 10% of positions with the largest KL divergence between the RL and base next-token distributions (the high-KL positions of the main text); it depends only on the two distributions, not on the token the base model sampled. The mismatch label marks positions where the RL model’s top-1 token differs from the token the base model sampled. This is not the criterion of rl-replace, which compares the two models’ top-1 tokens: the mismatch label is also positive wherever the base model samples a token other than its own top-1, even if the two distributions are identical.

Results.

High-KL positions are highly predictable from the base model’s own confidence (Table 12). Under the KL label, every confidence feature reaches an AUROC of 0.94–0.96, and the gate trained on all features reaches 0.969 / 0.980, with a precision of 0.54 / 0.62 at 90% recall. Position and token rank carry almost no information (0.53–0.57): whether a position diverges depends on how unsure the base model is there, not on where it falls in the response. Under the mismatch label, the chosen log-prob alone reaches 0.993 on both years. This number overstates how well the positions used by rl-replace can be located: a low chosen log-prob means the base model sampled a token other than its own top-1, which makes the mismatch label positive almost by construction. Our conclusions therefore rest on the KL label.

The numbers depend on the label. With a label defined as the 10% of positions with the lowest log⁡pRL−log⁡pbase\log p_{\text{RL}}-\log p_{\text{base}}, the best single feature drops to 0.63 on a separate set of 1,324 MATH problems; relabelling the same data with the KL label raises entropy to 0.95. Because most tokens have a positive log-probability difference, the lowest 10% is a noisy label. We therefore use the KL label, which depends only on the two models’ next-token distributions.

Implication.

The base model knows where it is uncertain: its confidence ranks the positions at which the RL model changes the next-token distribution most, with an AUROC of up to 0.98. What the base-only strategies we tested do not supply is which token to use there. Gate-MCMC resamples at these positions and does not help (§3.2), and rules that insert fixed tokens at similar positions hurt (§3.5). Locating these positions is comparatively easy; making the decisions is what the RL model contributes.

Appendix F What and Where the RL Model Replaces

This appendix gives the details behind §3.3 and §3.5. We first describe the replacements in all 1,920 rl-replace responses of the main run, and then look closely at the 19 AIME problems on which the base model fails all 16 samples while rl-replace solves at least one, and the 38 successful rl-replace responses on them.

F.1 All responses

How many tokens are replaced.

The per-response replace rate is 4.51% on AIME 2024, 4.69% on AIME 2025, 4.31% on AIME 2022 and 4.67% on AIME 2023; weighted by tokens it is 3.84%, 4.18%, 3.99% and 4.00%. A response contains about 246–261 replacements. Correct responses have a lower replace rate than incorrect ones (3.96% against 4.67%). Although only about 4% of the tokens come from the RL model, the responses take on its length: rl-replace responses average 6,217 tokens, close to the RL model’s 6,504 and nearly twice the base model’s 3,248.

Where.

All 1,920 responses are replaced at the first position, always by “Alright”. The base token it replaces is mostly “To” (51.5%) or “Assistant” (42.8%), and the most frequent replacement at position 2 is “let”→\to“I” (976 times). On MATH-500, 94.8% of the responses are replaced at the first position. After the opening, replacements are densest early in the response. Splitting each response into ten equal parts, the replace rate in each part is 6.0, 5.1, 4.4, 4.0, 3.7, 3.4, 3.3, 3.1, 3.2 and 3.8%, so the first tenth has nearly twice the density of the second half. The 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles of the relative position of a replacement are 0.06, 0.17, 0.40, 0.70 and 0.89.

What.

The replacements form a long tail: the main run contains 83,710 distinct base→\toRL token pairs and 6,376 distinct RL tokens, and the 100 most frequent pairs account for only 16.9% of all replacements. The most frequent pairs are “.\n\n”→\to“.” (4,009), “the”→\to“\(” (3,781), “the”→\to“we” (2,676), “Perhaps”→\to“Maybe” (1,309), “I”→\to“we” (1,213) and “So”→\to“Wait” (872). The tokens the RL model inserts most often are “the” (18,123), “\(” (17,768), “we” (10,339), “###” (9,928) and “But” (5,361). Reflective words become far more frequent: “Wait” appears 0.30 times per base response and 5.74 times per rl-replace response, and “Re” is inserted by the RL model 2,204 times but replaced only 288 times.

F.2 Successful responses on problems missed by all 16 base samples

Problems.

Figure 6 summarizes the 19 problems on which the base model fails all 16 samples but rl-replace solves at least one. Panel (a) shows the number of successful rl-replace samples for each problem. Fifteen of the 19 problems are solved by only one or two samples, while AIME 2025 Problem 4 stands out with 10 successes. Panel (b) shows the mean number of text-changing replacements in the successful responses for each problem. Across all 38 successful responses, the mean is about 240 replacements; this overall mean weights each problem by its number of successful samples.

Position in the response.

Table 13 splits the replacements by their relative position in the response. They are densest in the first fifth of the response and sparsest between 50% and 80%, with a slight rise in the last tenth.

Direction of the replacements.

Table 4 in the main text merges categories that occur in both directions. Table 14 separates them. The RL model moves text into LaTeX more often than out of it (607 against 467) and introduces a first-person subject more often than it removes one (292 against 142), but both directions are common, so it has no fixed preference for either style.

Frequent replacement pairs.

Table 15 lists the most frequent pairs by function. At the first position every one of the 38 responses replaces the base model’s opening with “Alright”, and in 25 of them the token at position 2 is also replaced, turning “let” into “I” and giving “Alright, I have this problem”. Some pairs only change style, such as “perhaps” →\to “maybe” (18 times). Number replacements have no fixed direction; the most frequent pairs are 2→\to1 (16), 2→\to4 (12), 2→\to6 (11), 1→\to2 (10) and 0→\to1 (10).

Excerpts.

The following excerpts from successful rl-replace responses show the replaced token in brackets. Where the base model’s greedy token opens a new section after a result, the RL model’s token is a pause, followed by a check:

CE = 104
[Wait], but let’s check the calculation more precisely.

Here the base model’s greedy token is “###”, the start of a new header. Similarly, after a total is computed:

Total = 404 + 405 = 809.
[Wait], but we need to ensure that we are not double-counting.

The text that follows such a pause often states the problem explicitly, for example “Wait, that’s not correct. Let’s think again.” or “Wait, this is inconsistent. Maybe I need to re-examine the small cases.”, and a pause is sometimes followed by a new header such as “### Re-examining the Problem”. Replacing “So” by “But” turns a conclusion into a check, as in “[But] Alice can also remove 4 tokens, which is impossible. So, Bob cannot win.” Number replacements fix values that the problem’s constraints rule out. In a game where a player may remove one or four tokens, the base model writes 2 at the bracketed positions, and the RL model’s tokens give

…or she can try to remove [4] tokens, but she can’t because there’s only [1] token.

In a coordinate-geometry problem, the base model’s “DA = 0” becomes “DA = [6], so point D = (0, 6)”. In each case the replaced token depends on what has been derived so far, which is what the fixed rules of §3.5 cannot see.

Appendix G Further Base-Only Interventions

Section 3.5 summarizes several interventions besides the “Wait” and “Re” rules. Figure 7 compares their effects on pass@1 and pass@16. All interventions act on the base model alone and are evaluated on the 120 AIME problems with 16 samples per problem. The bars show changes relative to the base model, whose pass@1 and pass@16 are 10.00% and 30.00%, respectively; the score columns give the absolute values.

These interventions do not reproduce the improvements achieved by rl-replace. Most lower pass@1, and all lower pass@16. The first-person bias lowers pass@1 by 1.3–1.5 percentage points, within the variation between independent base runs (§4.2). Greedy and low-temperature decoding of the first 100 tokens leave pass@1 close to the base level while lowering pass@16. In the greedy condition, all 16 samples share the same initial 100 tokens. Adding “Alright” before the greedy prefix raises pass@1 by about 1.2 points over the greedy prefix alone, in line with the opening effect of §3.4. This setting reaches 10.83% pass@1, but its pass@16 remains below the base model at 26.67%. The entropy rule with a single low threshold fires in only 13 of the 1,920 responses, and the two-sided rule in 301.

How often “Wait” is inserted.

The top-5 rule inserts “Wait” 1.64 times per response on average, and 76.7% of the responses receive no insertion at all. Once the rule fires it tends to fire again, often four to ten times in the same response. Accuracy falls with the number of insertions: 7.95% (117 of 1,472) for responses with none, 1.81% (3 of 166) for one to five, and 0 for the 282 responses with six or more. On the 36 problems the base model can solve, responses without an insertion are correct 26.8% of the time and responses with one only 2.0%. The base model writes “Wait” 0.30 times per response on its own, while rl-replace writes it 5.74 times and the RL model about 5.7 times and benefits from it, so the number of “Wait”s is not what separates helpful from harmful use.

Appendix H Additional Details on Accuracy and Coverage

Section 3.6 presents the large-kk results, with the Qwen3-4B curves in Figure 5 and results for both Qwen model sizes in Table 6. This appendix describes the response-level mixture and the temperature sensitivity of the Qwen3-4B RL baseline.

Response-level mixture.

For each problem, every attempt independently selects the RL model with probability 0.92 and the base model with probability 0.08. The selected model alone generates the complete response, using the evaluation prompt of Appendix B, temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95, and a maximum of 8,192 generated tokens. No generated prefix is shared between attempts.

The mixture therefore combines the models across complete responses, whereas rl-replace combines their token choices within each response. The weight 0.92 is chosen to approximately match rl-replace at pass@1: the independently generated mixture obtains 19.00%, compared with 18.98% for rl-replace. Its pass@16 and pass@256 are 38.78% and 61.45%, respectively. Figure 5a connects these three reported budgets with a dashed line. The paired problem-level bootstrap interval for the pass@256 difference is given in Table 10.

H.1 Temperature sensitivity of the RL baseline

We evaluate the Qwen3-4B RL model at temperatures 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8 on all 120 AIME problems. Top-pp is fixed at 0.95, and all conditions use the same evaluation prompt and 8,192-token output limit. Figure 8 reports pass@1, pass@16, pass@64, and pass@256.

The original temperature of 0.6 yields the highest RL pass@256 among the tested settings, at 61.40%. Lowering the temperature to 0.4 gives 58.25%, while increasing it to 0.8 gives 59.10%. rl-replace, evaluated at temperature 0.6, reaches 67.50%, exceeding the highest observed RL value by 6.10 percentage points. For rl-replace, temperature applies only to base-model sampling at agreement positions; disagreement positions use the RL model’s greedy token.

This comparison is limited to the three tested RL temperatures at a fixed top-pp. It does not characterize other decoding settings or the temperature sensitivity of rl-replace.

Appendix I Qualitative Analyses

I.1 The opening on the hardest problems

Section 3.4 measures the first token on all 120 problems. Here we look at the hardest ones: the eight problems on which both the base model and the RL model fail all 16 samples while rl-replace solves at least one. Table 16 counts correct responses out of 8×16=1288\times 16=128.

Forcing the opening solves two or three of these problems once each, while rl-replace solves all eight. Because the problems were selected by rl-replace’s success, its count is biased upward: with 256 samples its accuracy on them falls from 9.4% to 3.6%, so we neither compute a recovery rate nor count these problems as evidence that rl-replace solves problems beyond the RL model’s reach. The comparison only shows that on the hardest problems the opening alone does very little, in line with §3.4.

I.2 Two worked examples

We show parts of two rl-replace responses. Tokens in bold are chosen by the RL model, at positions where the greedy choices of the two models differ; every other token is sampled from the base model.

A pause before an overlap check.

AIME 2025 Problem 4 asks for the number of ordered pairs (x,y)(x,y) of integers between −100-100 and 100100, inclusive, with 12​x2−x​y−6​y2=012x^{2}-xy-6y^{2}=0 (answer 117). The base model fails all 16 samples and never answers 117; its most common answer is 168 (6 samples). rl-replace answers correctly in 10 samples and the RL model in 15. The base model can factor the equation as (3​x+2​y)​(4​x−3​y)=0(3x+2y)(4x-3y)=0 and so find the two families of solutions, but it never checks whether they overlap, and two of its samples answer 118.

The rl-replace response below has 2,085 tokens, of which the RL model chooses 84 (4.0%). It counts 51 pairs in one family and 67 in the other. At the next position the base model’s greedy token is “###”, which opens a new section header, and the RL model’s token is “Wait”, the only “Wait” in the response:

The rest of the check is mostly the base model’s own text: it solves the two equations, finds that only (0,0)(0,0) lies in both families, and answers 117. This is the ###→\toWait pattern of §3.5.

A doubt that is not followed through.

The second problem shows the same kind of replacement on a problem that no condition solves. Points A,B,C,DA,B,C,D lie on the hyperbola x220−y224=1\frac{x^{2}}{20}-\frac{y^{2}}{24}=1 and form a rhombus whose diagonals meet at the origin; the task is to find the greatest real number that is less than B​D2BD^{2} for all such rhombi (AIME 2024 Problem 9, answer 480). The base model, rl-replace and the RL model each fail all 16 samples, and 80 is the most common answer in each. Base responses open with “We are given the hyperbola…” or “To solve the problem, we’ll follow these steps:” and list steps at once; one of them concludes that B​D2BD^{2} is unbounded.

In the rl-replace response below (1,611 tokens, 76 chosen by the RL model, 4.7%), the first token is “Alright”. The response lists the properties of a rhombus, including that its diagonals bisect each other at right angles, and then places the diagonals on the coordinate axes. At a position where the base model’s greedy token is “So”, the RL model’s token is “Wait”:

The doubt is correct, since the diagonals need not lie on the axes, but the response keeps the assumption, obtains B​D2=960BD^{2}=960, and answers 959. In the first example the base model carries the check through; here it does not.

I.3 Where the RL model disagrees most

To see what the strongest disagreements look like, we inspected base-model responses on a set of 1,324 MATH problems at the positions where the RL model assigns the sampled token a much lower log-probability than the base model does. Two kinds of context recur. The first is a template opening such as “Let’s solve the problem step by step” or “First, let’s consider…”, where the base model itself is often unsure of its token and the RL model puts most of its probability on other tokens, in line with the opening change of §3.4. The second is a premature conclusion in the middle of a derivation, such as “So, the roots are:” before the roots have been derived; connectives such as “Given that…” or “Since a<ba<b…” are marked in the same way, less strongly. At an equals sign or a LaTeX command the RL model usually agrees with the token itself, and the disagreement concerns what follows: the value on the right of the equals sign, or how an expression is written, such as the grouping when completing the square. These observations are qualitative and are not used for any number in the main text.
